label: coniektore
title: Conjecture
body_md:
\label{coniektore}
Every nonzero subspace $V\subset\ell_\infty^N$ with $\lambda(V)<\frac43$
satisfies
$$
d(V,\ell_\infty^{\dim V})\leq\frac{\lambda(V)}{4-3\lambda(V)}.
$$
head: environment

label: domina
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{domina}
    Let $A=(a_{ij})\in\mathbb{K
    }^{n\times n}$, where $\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{C}.$ If $A$ is strictly diagonally dominant, that is,
$$ 
|a_{ii}|>\sum_{j\ne i}|a_{ij}|, \qquad i\in [1:n] 
$$
then $A$ is nonsingular.
head: environment
name: L\'evy-Desplanques, see e.g.\

label: rankus
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{rankus}
Let $A=(a_{ij})\in \mathbb{K}^{N\times N},$ where $\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{C}.$ If 
$$
2|a_{ii}|>\sum_{j\ne i}|a_{ij}|, \qquad i\in [1:N] 
$$
then ${\rm rank}(A)\geq \tfrac{N}{2}.$
head: environment

label: kombin
title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose, to the contrary, that $r:=\mathrm{rank}(A)<\tfrac{N}{2}$. The assumption implies $a_{ii}\neq 0$ for all $i$, so $A\neq 0$ and $r\geq 1$. Among all $r\times r$ submatrices of $A$, choose one, say $A_{I,J}$, with maximal $|\det A_{I,J}|$. Since $\mathrm{rank}(A)=r$, we have $\det A_{I,J}\neq 0$.  In particular, the columns $a_j$, $j\in J$, of $A$  form a basis of the column space of $A$. Hence, for every $k\in J':=[1:N]\setminus J$, there exist scalars $c_j^k\in \mathbb{K}$, $j\in J$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{kombin}
a_k=\sum_{j\in J}c_j^ka_j .
\end{equation}
We claim that $|c_j^k|\leq 1$ for all $j\in J$ and $k\in J'$. Indeed, fix such $j$ and $k$ and put $J_j^k := (J \cup \{k\}) \setminus \{j\}$.  By \eqref{kombin} and multilinearity of the determinant, $|\det A_{I,J_j^k}| = |c_j^k| \cdot |\det A_{I,J}|$. The maximality of $|\det A_{I,J}|$ implies
$$
|\det A_{I,J}|\geq |\det A_{I,J_j^k}|=|c_j^k||\det A_{I,J}|.
$$
Since $\det A_{I,J}\neq 0$, this gives $|c_j^k|\leq 1$, as required. Now let $k \in J'$. By \eqref{kombin}  and the above observation, we get
$$
|a_{kk}|\leq \sum_{j\in J}|c_j^k||a_{kj}|\leq \sum_{j\in J}|a_{kj}|.
$$
Since $k \notin J$, this and the lemma's assumption imply
$$
\sum_{\substack{j\in J'\\ j\neq k}}|a_{kj}|=\sum_{j\ne k}|a_{kj}|-\sum_{j\in J}|a_{kj}|<2|a_{kk}|-|a_{kk}|=|a_{kk}|.
$$
Thus the submatrix $A_{J',J'}$ is strictly diagonally dominant and hence, by Theorem~\ref{domina}, nonsingular. It follows that
$$
N-r=|J'|\leq \mathrm{rank}(A)=r.
$$
Hence $\tfrac{N}{2}\leq r$,  a contradiction.\\
~\\
The previous rank estimate can now be applied to the complementary projection. As a consequence, a small-norm projection may have only a limited number of diagonal entries that are not close to one.

\begin{lemma}\label{conajmniej}
Let $V\subset \ell_\infty^N$ be a subspace of dimension $N-m$, and let
$P=(p_{ij})_{i,j=1}^N$ be a projection onto $V$ satisfying
$\|P\|\leq 1+\varepsilon,$ for some $\varepsilon\geq0.$ Then
$|p_{ii}|\geq 1-\varepsilon$ for at least $N-2m$ indices $i\in[1:N]$.
\end{lemma}
head: manual

label: conajmniej
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{conajmniej}
Let $V\subset \ell_\infty^N$ be a subspace of dimension $N-m$, and let
$P=(p_{ij})_{i,j=1}^N$ be a projection onto $V$ satisfying
$\|P\|\leq 1+\varepsilon,$ for some $\varepsilon\geq0.$ Then
$|p_{ii}|\geq 1-\varepsilon$ for at least $N-2m$ indices $i\in[1:N]$.
head: environment

label: lem1
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $Q={\rm Id}-P.$ Since $P$ is a projection onto a subspace of dimension $N-m$, the
complementary projection $Q$ has rank $m$. Denote by
$ I:=\{i\in[1:N]: |p_{ii}|<1-\varepsilon\}$
the set of indices where the desired inequality does not hold. Let
$k=|I|$. We claim that $k\leq 2m$. Indeed, for every $i\in I$,
$ |q_{ii}| = |1-p_{ii}| \geq 1-|p_{ii}|> \varepsilon.$  Furthermore, from $\|P\|\leq 1+\varepsilon$ we get $ |1-q_{ii}|+\sum_{j\neq i}|q_{ij}|
\leq 1+\varepsilon. $ Combining this with the fact that
$ |1-q_{ii}|\geq 1-|q_{ii}|$ implies
$$
\sum_{j\neq i}|q_{ij}|
\leq
\varepsilon+|q_{ii}|
<2|q_{ii}|.
$$
Now let
$\widetilde{Q}=(q_{ij})_{i,j\in I}.$
 By  the latter and Lemma~\ref{rankus} 
 $$
\frac{k}{2}\leq {\rm rank}(\widetilde{Q})\leq {\rm rank(Q)}= m.
$$
Thus, $k \leq 2m$, as claimed.\\
~\\
In the codimension-two case, the previous estimate leaves at most four coordinates uncontrolled.  This leads us to the geometry of two-dimensional subspaces of $\ell_\infty^4$.
\begin{lemma}\label{lem1}
Let $f,g\in \ell_1^4$ be linearly independent and set
$ V=\ker f\cap\ker g. $
Suppose that there exists $k\in[1:4]$ such that
$ 3|\Delta_{lk}|<\|\Delta_l\|_1  $  for all $l\neq k,$
then there exists $v\in V$ such that $|v_k|=1$ and $|v_i|\leq\frac12$
for all $i\neq k.$
\end{lemma}
head: manual

label: lem1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem1}
Let $f,g\in \ell_1^4$ be linearly independent and set
$ V=\ker f\cap\ker g. $
Suppose that there exists $k\in[1:4]$ such that
$ 3|\Delta_{lk}|<\|\Delta_l\|_1  $  for all $l\neq k,$
then there exists $v\in V$ such that $|v_k|=1$ and $|v_i|\leq\frac12$
for all $i\neq k.$
head: environment

label: inq123
title: Proof
body_md:
By permuting the coordinates, we may assume that $k=4$. We first establish that
$
{\rm span}\{\Delta_1,\Delta_2,\Delta_3\}=V^\perp.
$
Indeed, each $\Delta_l$ belongs to
$
V^\perp={\rm span}\{f,g\},
$
and the inequalities
\begin{equation}\label{inq123}
3|\Delta_{l4}|<\|\Delta_l\|_1,
\qquad l=1,2,3,
\end{equation}
ensure that $\Delta_1,\Delta_2,\Delta_3$ are all nonzero. Assume that their span is a proper subspace of $V^\perp$. Since
$\dim V^\perp=2$, their span must then be one-dimensional. Thus
$\Delta_1$ is linearly dependent with both $\Delta_2$ and $\Delta_3$,
which yields
$\Delta_{12}=\Delta_{13}=0.$
As $\Delta_{11}=0$, it follows that
$\|\Delta_1\|_1=|\Delta_{14}|.$
which contradicts \eqref{inq123}. Moreover, for every $i\in[1:3]$, at least one of
$\Delta_{1i},\Delta_{2i},\Delta_{3i}$ is nonzero. Otherwise, since
$\Delta_1,\Delta_2,\Delta_3$ span $V^\perp$, we would have
$f_i=g_i=0$ for some $i$, and therefore $\Delta_i=0$, contradicting
\eqref{inq123}.
For $h\in \ell_1^4$ by $\widetilde{h}$ we denote the restriction of the functional to subspace $V.$ 
First, consider the case where $\widetilde{e_1},\widetilde{e_2},\widetilde{e_3}$ do not
span $V^*$. Since $\dim V^*=2$, their span has dimension one and consequently the intersection of kernels of these functionals has dimension one. Hence  $(0,0,0,1)\in V$ and is our desired vector.\\
Now assume that vectors $\widetilde{e_1},\widetilde{e_2},\widetilde{e_3}$ span whole space $V^{*}.$  First observe that $\widetilde{e_4}$ can not be equal to $0.$ Indeed if so,  then ${\rm span}\{\Delta_1,\Delta_2,\Delta_3\}={\rm span}\{e_4\}\subsetneq V^{\perp},$ a contradiction. We will show that $\widetilde{e_4}\notin {\rm conv}\{ \pm2\widetilde{e_1},\pm2\widetilde{e_2},\pm2\widetilde{e_3}\}=:C.$ For the contrary assume that $\widetilde{e_4}\in C.$ By the definition of set $C$ there exists $t\geq1$ such that $t\widetilde{e_4}\in\partial C.$ By Carath\'eodory theorem there exists $i,j\in[1:3]$ and $a,b\in\mathbb{R},$ such that $|a|+|b|=1$ and  $t\widetilde{e_4}=2a\widetilde{e_i}+2b\widetilde{e_j}.$ Then $te_4-2ae_i-2be_j\in V^\perp.$ Let $l\in [1:3]\setminus \{i,j\}.$ Then at least one $\Delta_{il} $ or $\Delta_{jl} $ has to be nonzero. Hence 
$$
te_4-2ae_i-2be_j=\frac{t\Delta_l}{\Delta_{l4}}
$$
and consequently 
$$
|a|+|b|=\frac{t(|\Delta_{li}|+|\Delta_{lj}|)}{2|\Delta_{l4}|}=\frac{t(\|\Delta_l\|_1-|\Delta_{l4}|)}{2|\Delta_{l4}|}>t\geq 1,
$$
a contradiction. Now, by the separation theorem there exist $v\in V=(V^*)^*$ such that 
$$
|v_4|=|\widetilde{e_4}(v)|>\max\{|h(v)|:\; h\in C\}\geq 2|\widetilde{e_l}(v)|=2|v_l|\;\; \textrm{ for all } l\in[1:3].
$$
Dividing $v$ by $|v_4|$ gives the desired vector.\\
~\\

\begin{lemma}\label{godorbed}
Let $f,g\in \ell_1^4$ be linearly independent and set
$ V=\ker f\cap\ker g. $
Suppose that there exist $i,j\in[1:4]$ such that $i\neq j$ and
$ 3|\Delta_{ij}|\leq \|\Delta_j\|_1  $ 
then there exists $v\in V$ such that $\|v\|_{\infty}=1$ and $|v_l|\leq\frac12$
for all $l\notin\{i,j\}.$
\end{lemma}
head: manual

label: godorbed
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{godorbed}
Let $f,g\in \ell_1^4$ be linearly independent and set
$ V=\ker f\cap\ker g. $
Suppose that there exist $i,j\in[1:4]$ such that $i\neq j$ and
$ 3|\Delta_{ij}|\leq \|\Delta_j\|_1  $ 
then there exists $v\in V$ such that $\|v\|_{\infty}=1$ and $|v_l|\leq\frac12$
for all $l\notin\{i,j\}.$
head: environment

label: beechandwitch
title: Proof
body_md:
By relabeling the coordinates, it is enough to assume that  $i=1$ and $j=2$. Suppose first that $\Delta_{12}=0$. Then the restrictions of $f$ and
$g$ to ${\rm span}\{e_1,e_2\}$ are linearly dependent, and hence there
exists a nonzero vector $v\in V$ with $v_3=v_4=0.$
After normalization $v$, we obtain $\|v\|_\infty=1$, and the conclusion
follows.\\
If $\Delta_{12}\neq 0,$ then $V=\ker \Delta_1\cap\ker \Delta_2,$ and by the definition of space V 
$$u:=(\Delta_{23},-\Delta_{13},\Delta_{12},0)\in V \;\;\;\textrm{ and } \;\;\;w:=(\Delta_{24},-\Delta_{14},0,\Delta_{12})\in V$$  
and consequently 
$$
v:=\frac{1}{|\Delta_{23}|+|\Delta_{24}|}({\rm sgn}(\Delta_{23})u+{\rm sgn}(\Delta_{24})w )\in V.
$$
Moreover $\|v\|_{\infty}\geq 1$ and for $l\notin \{1,2\} $
$$
|v_l|\leq\frac{|\Delta_{12}|}{|\Delta_{23}|+|\Delta_{24}|}=\frac{|\Delta_{12}|}{\|\Delta_2\|-|\Delta_{12}|}\leq \frac{1}{2}.
$$
once more by renorming vector $v$ we yield the thesis.\\
~\\
Combining the two previous lemmas gives the following theorem.
\begin{thm}\label{beechandwitch}
Let $f,g\in \ell_1^4$ be linearly independent and set
$ V=\ker f\cap\ker g. $
There exist two disjoint sets $I, J\subset[1:4]$ and vectors $v,w\in V$ such that 
$$
\|v\|_\infty=\|w\|_\infty=1 \;\;\;\textit{ and }\;\;\; \max_{i\notin I}|v_i|\leq\frac{1}{2}, \; \max_{i\notin J}|w_i|\leq\frac{1}{2}.
$$
\end{thm}
head: manual

label: beechandwitch
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{beechandwitch}
Let $f,g\in \ell_1^4$ be linearly independent and set
$ V=\ker f\cap\ker g. $
There exist two disjoint sets $I, J\subset[1:4]$ and vectors $v,w\in V$ such that 
$$
\|v\|_\infty=\|w\|_\infty=1 \;\;\;\textit{ and }\;\;\; \max_{i\notin I}|v_i|\leq\frac{1}{2}, \; \max_{i\notin J}|w_i|\leq\frac{1}{2}.
$$
head: environment

label: base
title: Proof
body_md:
For convenience, we say that a set $I\subset [1:4]$ is good if there exists vector $v\in V$ such that $\|v\|_{\infty}=1$ and $\max_{i\notin I}|v_i|\leq\frac{1}{2},$ and bad otherwise.  Assume, to the contrary, that no two disjoint sets
are good. Thus, in each of the three complementary pairs
$$
\{1,2\},\{3,4\};\qquad
\{1,3\},\{2,4\};\qquad
\{1,4\},\{2,3\},
$$
at least one set is bad. It follows that either there exist three distinct
indices $i,j,k\in[1:4]$ such that
$
\{i,j\},\;\{j,k\},\;\{k,i\}
$
are all bad, or there exists an index $i\in[1:4]$ such that
$
\{i,k\}
$
is bad for every $k\neq i$.
We begin with the first case. After relabeling the coordinates, we may
assume that $\{1,2\},\{2,3\},\{3,1\}$ are bad. By badness of $\{1,2\}$ and $\{3,1\}$ using  Lemma \ref{godorbed} we get
\begin{align*}
    \|\Delta_1\|_1<3|\Delta_{12}| 
    \;\;\;\textrm{ and }\;\;\;
    \|\Delta_1\|_1<3|\Delta_{13}|. 
\end{align*}
Adding the above inequalities yields
\begin{align*}
    2\|\Delta_1\|_1<3|\Delta_{12}|+3|\Delta_{13}|=3\|\Delta_1\|_1-3|\Delta_{14}|
\end{align*}
and consequently 
$$
3|\Delta_{14}|<\|\Delta_1\|_1.
$$
Analogously by badness of $\{1,2\}, \{2,3\}$ and $\{1,3\}, \{2,3\}$ we get
\begin{align*}
    3|\Delta_{24}|<\|\Delta_2\|_1 \;\;\;\textrm{ and }\;\;\;  3|\Delta_{34}|<\|\Delta_3\|_1.
\end{align*}
Therefore by Lemma \ref{lem1} set $\{4\}$ is good. Set $\{1,2,3\}$ also will be good because $V$ is two dimensional space, so there has to exist $v\in V$ such that $v_4=0,$ and $\|v\|_{\infty}=1,$ a contradiction.\\
Now consider the remaining case and assume that for some $i\in[1:4]$ every set $\{i,k\}$ is bad if $k\neq i.$ By Lemma \ref{godorbed} for all $k\neq i$
$$
\|\Delta_i\|_{1}<3|\Delta_{ik}|.
$$
Adding these inequalities, we obtain $3\|\Delta_i\|_1<3\|\Delta_i\|_1,$ a contradiction.\\
~\\
The preceding geometric argument, together with Lemma~\ref{conajmniej}, yields the following result for projections onto codimension-two subspaces.
\begin{thm}\label{base}
Let $N \geq 4$, and let $V \subset \ell_\infty^N$ be a subspace of dimension $N-2$.
Let $P = (p_{ij})_{i,j=1}^N : \ell_\infty^N \to V$  be a projection satisfying
$\|P\| \leq 1 + \varepsilon$ for some $ \varepsilon \geq 0 $.
Then there exist pairwise disjoint nonempty sets
$A_1,\ldots,A_{N-2}\subset[1:N]$ and indices $k_i\in A_i$ such that
$$
\sum_{l\in A_i}|p_{k_i l}|\geq1-\varepsilon,\;\;
{\it for }\;\; i\in[1:N-2].
$$
\end{thm}

label: base
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{base}

Let $P = (p_{ij})_{i,j=1}^N : \ell_\infty^N \to V$  be a projection satisfying
$\|P\| \leq 1 + \varepsilon$ for some $ \varepsilon \geq 0 $.
Then there exist pairwise disjoint nonempty sets
$A_1,\ldots,A_{N-2}\subset[1:N]$ and indices $k_i\in A_i$ such that

head: environment

label: Bazur
title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{conajmniej}, after relabeling the coordinates we may assume that
$
|p_{ii}|\geq1-\varepsilon,$ for $i\in[5:N].$
Hence $\{5\},\ldots,\{N\}$ already give $N-4$ of the required sets.
Set
$$
\widetilde W:=\{x\in V:x_i=0,\ i\in[5:N]\}.
$$
Since $\dim\widetilde W\geq2$, choose a two-dimensional subspace
$W\subset\widetilde W$ and identify it with its restriction to the first
four coordinates. By the Theorem~\ref{beechandwitch}, there exist disjoint nonempty sets
$I,J\subset[1:4]$ and $v,w\in W$ such that
$$
\|v\|_\infty=\|w\|_\infty=1,
\qquad
|v_i|\leq\frac12\ (i\notin I),
\qquad
|w_i|\leq\frac12\ (i\notin J).
$$
Let $i\in I$ be such that $|v_i|=1$.
As $v\in V$, we have $Pv=v$, and therefore
\begin{align*}
1
=|v_i|
&=
\Big|\sum_{l=1}^N p_{il}v_l\Big| 
\leq
\sum_{l\in I}|p_{il}||v_l|
+
\sum_{l\notin I}|p_{il}||v_l| 
\leq
\sum_{l\in I}|p_{il}|
+
\frac12\sum_{l\notin I}|p_{il}| \\
&=
\frac12\sum_{l\in I}|p_{il}|
+
\frac12\sum_{l=1}^N|p_{il}| 
\leq
\frac12\sum_{l\in I}|p_{il}|
+
\frac12(1+\varepsilon).
\end{align*}
Hence
$$
\sum_{l\in I}|p_{il}|\geq1-\varepsilon.
$$
The analogous argument gives $j\in J$ such that
$$
\sum_{l\in J}|p_{jl}|\geq1-\varepsilon.
$$
Thus $I,J,\{5\},\ldots,\{N\}$ have the required properties.
\begin{thm}\label{Bazur}
Let $V\subset\ell_\infty^N$ be a subspace of dimension $N-2$. If
$\lambda(V)<\frac43,$ then
$$
d(V,\ell_\infty^{N-2})
\leq
\frac{\lambda(V)}{4-3\lambda(V)}.
$$
\end{thm}
head: manual

label: Bazur
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Bazur}
Let $V\subset\ell_\infty^N$ be a subspace of dimension $N-2$. If
$\lambda(V)<\frac43,$ then
$$
d(V,\ell_\infty^{N-2})
\leq
\frac{\lambda(V)}{4-3\lambda(V)}.
$$
head: environment

label: qdiag
title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\lambda(V)<\frac43,$ there exists $0\leq\varepsilon < \frac13 $ such that $\lambda(V)=1+\varepsilon.$ If $\varepsilon=0$ it is well known that  $d(V,\ell_\infty^{N-2})=1$ (see e.g. \cite{BB}) and the above statement is true. So it is enough to consider $0<\varepsilon < \frac13. $ Since $\lambda(V)=\lambda(V,\ell_{\infty}^N)$  there exists   a projection $P:\ell_\infty^N\to V$ such that
$$
\|P\|= 1+\varepsilon=\lambda(V).
$$
By Theorem~\ref{base}, there exist pairwise disjoint nonempty sets
$A_1,\ldots,A_{N-2}\subset[1:N]$ and indices $k_i\in A_i$ such that
$$
\sum_{j\in A_i}|p_{k_i j}|\geq1-\varepsilon,
\qquad i\in[1:N-2].
$$
Let $p_j$ denote the $j$-th column of $P$ and set
$$
q_i:=\sum_{j\in A_i}{\rm sgn}(p_{k_i j})p_j.
$$
Since each $p_j$ belongs to $V$, we have $q_i\in V$. Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{qdiag}
(q_i)_{k_i}
=
\sum_{j\in A_i}{\rm sgn}(p_{k_i j})p_{k_i j}
=
\sum_{j\in A_i}|p_{k_i j}|
\geq1-\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
The disjointness of the sets $A_i$ implies that, for every
$l\in[1:N]$,
\begin{align}
\sum_{i=1}^{N-2}|(q_i)_l|
\leq
\sum_{i=1}^{N-2}\sum_{j\in A_i}|p_{lj}| 
\leq
\sum_{j=1}^N|p_{lj}|
\leq1+\varepsilon.
\label{qineq}
\end{align}
We first show that $q_1,\ldots,q_{N-2}$ are linearly independent.
Suppose that
$\sum_{i=1}^{N-2}a_iq_i=0$
and choose $m$ such that $|a_m|=\max_i|a_i|$. 
Then, using \eqref{qdiag} and \eqref{qineq}, we obtain
\begin{align*}
0 &= \Big| \sum_{i=1}^{N-2}a_i(q_i)_{k_m} \Big|
\geq |a_m||(q_m)_{k_m}|- \sum_{i\neq m}|a_i||(q_i)_{k_m}|
\geq |a_m|\Big( |(q_m)_{k_m}|- \sum_{i\neq m}|(q_i)_{k_m}|\Big)\\
&=|a_m| \Big( 2|(q_m)_{k_m}| - \sum_{i=1}^{N-2}|(q_i)_{k_m}| \Big)
\geq |a_m|\bigl(2(1-\varepsilon)-(1+\varepsilon)\bigr)
=|a_m|(1-3\varepsilon).
\end{align*}
Since $\varepsilon<\frac13$ we get $|a_m|=0,$ and consequently $a_i=0$ for all $i\in[1,N-2].$
Thus $q_1,\ldots,q_{N-2}$ are linearly independent and therefore form a basis of $V$.
Define isomorphism
$$
T:V\longrightarrow\ell_\infty^{N-2},
\qquad
T\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{N-2}a_iq_i\Big)
=
(a_1,\ldots,a_{N-2}).
$$
Let $a=(a_1,\ldots,a_{N-2})\in\ell_\infty^{N-2}$. By \eqref{qineq},
\begin{align*}
\|T^{-1}a\|_\infty
&= \Big\|\sum_{i=1}^{N-2}a_iq_i\Big\|_\infty
\leq \|a\|_\infty \max_{l\in[1:N]}\sum_{i=1}^{N-2}|(q_i)_l|
\leq
(1+\varepsilon)\|a\|_\infty.
\end{align*}
Thus
\begin{equation}\label{Tinverse}
\|T^{-1}\|\leq1+\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
On the other hand, choose $m$ such that $|a_m|=\|a\|_\infty$. Using
\eqref{qdiag} and \eqref{qineq} once again, we get
\begin{align*}
\Big\|\sum_{i=1}^{N-2}a_iq_i\Big\|_\infty
\geq \Big| \sum_{i=1}^{N-2}a_i(q_i)_{k_m} \Big|
\geq |a_m| \Big( 2|(q_m)_{k_m}|- \sum_{i=1}^{N-2}|(q_i)_{k_m}| \Big)
\geq (1-3\varepsilon)\|a\|_\infty.
\end{align*}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{Tnorm}
\|T\|\leq\frac1{1-3\varepsilon}.
\end{equation}
Combining \eqref{Tinverse} and \eqref{Tnorm}, we obtain
$$
d(V,\ell_\infty^{N-2})
\leq
\|T\|\,\|T^{-1}\|
\leq
\frac{1+\varepsilon}{1-3\varepsilon}=\frac{\lambda(V)}{4-3\lambda(V)}
$$
 as required.
head: manual

label: hypergeom
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{hypergeom}
Let $V=\ker f\subset\ell_\infty^N$, where
$0\neq f=(f_1,\ldots,f_N)\in\ell_1^N$. Then there exist
$N-1$ pairwise disjoint nonempty sets
$A_1,\ldots,A_{N-1}\subset[1:N]$ and vectors
$v^1,\ldots,v^{N-1}\in V$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{HilaryHahn}
\|v^i\|_\infty=1
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
|v^i_j|\leq\frac12
\quad\text{for }j\notin A_i.
\end{equation}
head: environment

label: counterhigher
title: Proof
body_md:
We may assume that $\|f\|_1=1$. First, we will show that if for some $i$
$3|f_i|\leq1,$ then $\{i\}$ has property \eqref{HilaryHahn}.
If $f_i=0$, then $e_i\in V$ and there is nothing to prove. Otherwise,
since $|f_i|\leq\frac12\sum_{j\neq i}|f_j|$ the vector
$ e_i-f_i\Big(\sum_{k\neq i}|f_k|\Big)^{-1}
\sum_{j\neq i}{\rm sgn}(f_j)e_j$
belongs to $V,$ and all coordinates except the $i$-th have
modulus at most $1/2$. Since $\sum_i|f_i|=1$, there can be at most two indices for which
$3|f_i|>1$. If there is at most one such index, we may take
$N-1$ singletons. If there are two, say $j$ and $k$, then all the
remaining singletons have the required property, while $\{j,k\}$ does
as well, since $f_ke_j-f_je_k\in V\setminus\{0\}$ and this vector is supported on $\{j,k\}$.\\
~\\
Combining this proposition with the initial observation in this
section gives
$$
d(V,\ell_\infty^{N-1})
\leq
\frac{\lambda(V)}{4-3\lambda(V)},
$$
for hyperplanes with $\lambda(V)<\frac43.$
It is natural to ask whether the geometric statement used in the proof
of Theorem~\ref{base} extends to higher codimensions. The following
example shows that this is not the case. In fact, its natural analog
fails for $n$-dimensional subspaces of $\ell_\infty^{2n}$ when
$n\geq3$.
\begin{prop}\label{counterhigher}
For every $n\geq3$ there exists an $n$-dimensional subspace
$W_n\subset\ell_\infty^{2n}$ such that there are no pairwise disjoint
nonempty sets $A_1,\ldots,A_n\subset[1:2n]$ and vectors
$w_1,\ldots,w_n\in W_n$ satisfying
$$
\|w_i\|_\infty=1
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
|w_i^j|\leq\frac12
\quad\text{for }j\notin A_i.
$$
\end{prop}

label: combiningWn
title: Proof
body_md:
Set vectors
\begin{equation*}
    u:=(1,\tfrac{4}{5},\tfrac{1}{4},-\tfrac{1}{4},-\tfrac{4}{5})\qquad {\rm and }\qquad v:=(0,\tfrac{3}{5},1,1,\tfrac{3}{5}) 
\end{equation*} and define space $V:={\rm span}\{u,v\}.$ We claim that every nonzero
$x\in V$ has at least three coordinates of modulus greater than
$\frac12\|x\|_\infty$. Let
$$
x:=au+bv =
\Big( a,\frac45a+\frac35b,\frac14a+b,
-\frac14a+b,-\frac45a+\frac35b \Big).
$$
Since changing the sign of either coefficient only permutes the
absolute values of the coordinates, we may assume that $a,b\geq0$.
Then $|x_4|\leq x_3$ and $|x_5|\leq x_2$, so
$\|x\|_\infty=\max\{x_1,x_2,x_3\}.$
Suppose that $\|x\|_{\infty}=|x_1|=x_1.$ Observe that $x_2-x_5=\tfrac{8}{5}x_1,$ and consequently
$$
\frac{8}{5}\|x\|_{\infty}=|x_2-x_5|\leq |x_2|+|x_5|\leq\|x\|_{\infty}+\min\{|x_2|,|x_5|\},
$$
which implies $|x_1|,|x_2|,|x_5|>\tfrac{1}{2}\|x\|_{\infty}.$\\
Assume now that $\|x\|_{\infty}=|x_2|.$ Observe that $13x_1+12x_3=20x_2,$ and consequently
$$
20\|x\|_{\infty}\leq 13\|x\|_{\infty}+12\min\{|x_1|,|x_3|\}
$$
which implies $|x_1|,|x_2|,|x_3|>\tfrac{1}{2}\|x\|_{\infty}.$\\
Finally let $\|x\|_{\infty}=|x_3|.$ Since $x_1,x_3\geq 0$, by the previous equality $|x_2|\geq\tfrac{12}{20}\|x\|_{\infty}.$ Moreover, $x_3=\frac{1}{2}x_1+x_4,$ and consequently $|x_3|\leq \frac{3}{2}\max\{|x_1|,|x_4|\},$ Hence $x_3$, $x_2$, and at least one of $x_1,x_4$ have modulus larger than $\tfrac{1}{2}\|x\|_\infty.$\\
For $n\geq3$, we set
$$
W_n:=\{(x,s,t_1,t_1,\ldots,t_{n-3},t_{n-3}):
       x\in V,\ s,t_1,\ldots,t_{n-3}\in\mathbb R\}.
$$
Clearly, $\dim W_n=n$. Suppose that sets $A_i$ and vectors $w^i$
satisfy the stated conditions. Choose $k_i\in A_i$ such that
$|w^i_{k_i}|=1$. Since the sets $A_i$ are pairwise disjoint,
the indices $k_1,\ldots,k_n$ are distinct.
If $k_i$ lies in one of the repeated pairs, both coordinates of that pair have modulus one in $w^i$ and must therefore belong to $A_i$. Consequently, each repeated pair contains at most one selected index. There are $n-3$ such pairs, and the only other coordinate outside $[1:5]$ is $6$. Hence at most $n-2$ of the selected indices lie outside $[1:5]$, so at least two lie in $[1:5]$.
The restrictions of the corresponding vectors to the first five
coordinates belong to $V$ and have norm one. Each therefore has
at least three coordinates of modulus greater than $1/2$, all
of which must belong to the corresponding set $A_i$. This is
impossible, since two disjoint subsets of $[1:5]$ cannot both
contain at least three elements.\\
~\\
Proposition~\ref{counterhigher} shows that the geometric argument used
in the proof of Theorem~\ref{base} does not extend to higher codimension.
It remains possible, however, that the conclusion of
Theorem~\ref{base}, which is all that is needed in the proof of
Theorem~\ref{Bazur}, continues to hold. For the spaces $W_n$ constructed
above this is indeed the case.\\
~\\
We keep the notation from the preceding proof.
\begin{prop}\label{combiningWn}
Let $n\geq3$, and let
$P=(p_{ij}):\ell_\infty^{2n}\to W_n$
be a projection satisfying
$$
\|P\|\leq1+\varepsilon,
\qquad 0\leq\varepsilon\leq\frac13.
$$
Then there exist pairwise disjoint nonempty sets
$A_1,\ldots,A_n\subset[1:2n]$ and indices $k_i\in A_i$ such that
$$
\sum_{j\in A_i}|p_{k_i j}|\geq1-\varepsilon,
\qquad i\in[1:n].
$$
\end{prop}

label: pairalternative
title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the submatrix $\widetilde P=(p_{ij})_{i,j=1}^5$. Observe that for $y\in\ell_\infty^5$,  $P(y,0,\ldots,0)\in W_n$, and consequently its first five
coordinates belong to $V$. These coordinates are precisely
$\widetilde P y$, and hence $\widetilde P$ maps $\ell_\infty^5$ into $V.$ Moreover, for every $x\in V$, the vector $(x,0,\ldots,0)$
belongs to $W_n$, and therefore
$P(x,0,\ldots,0)=(x,0,\ldots,0).$
Taking the first five coordinates gives $\widetilde Px=x$.
Thus $\widetilde P$ is a projection onto $V$, and
$\|\widetilde P\|\leq\|P\|\leq1+\varepsilon.$
We first show that
\begin{equation}\label{pairalternative}
\max\{|p_{21}|+|p_{22}|,\ |p_{51}|+|p_{55}|\}
\geq1-\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
Recall that $V={\rm span}\{u,v\}$ where
$$
 u=(1,\tfrac{4}{5},\tfrac{1}{4},-\tfrac{1}{4},-\tfrac{4}{5})\qquad {\rm and }\qquad v=(0,\tfrac{3}{5},1,1,\tfrac{3}{5}). 
 $$
For $z=(1,1,1,-1,-1)$, direct calculation gives
\begin{align*}
u+\tfrac13v-\tfrac25(e_1+e_2)-\tfrac14z
&=\Big(\tfrac7{20},\tfrac7{20},\tfrac13,\tfrac13,-\tfrac7{20}\Big),\\
-u+\tfrac13v-\tfrac25(e_5-e_1)+\tfrac14z
&=\Big(-\tfrac7{20},-\tfrac7{20},\tfrac13,\tfrac13,\tfrac7{20}\Big).
\end{align*}
Since $\|\widetilde P\|\leq1+\varepsilon$, the image of each of
these vectors under $\widetilde P$ has all coordinates bounded
in modulus by $\frac7{20}(1+\varepsilon)$. Thus, taking the second
coordinate of the first image and the fifth coordinate of the second,
we obtain
 \begin{align*}
1&\leq
\frac25(p_{21}+p_{22})
+\frac14(\widetilde Pz)_2+\frac7{20}(1+\varepsilon),\\
1
&\leq
\frac25(-p_{51}+p_{55})
-\frac14(\widetilde Pz)_5+\frac7{20}(1+\varepsilon).
\end{align*}
Since $\widetilde Pz\in V$, the definition of $V$ gives
$$
(\widetilde Pz)_2-(\widetilde Pz)_5
=\frac85(\widetilde Pz)_1.
$$
Moreover, $\|z\|_\infty=1$, so
$|(\widetilde Pz)_1|\leq1+\varepsilon$.
Adding the preceding inequalities therefore yields
\begin{align*}
2
&\leq
\frac25(p_{21}+p_{22}-p_{51}+p_{55})
+\frac25(\widetilde Pz)_1
+\frac7{10}(1+\varepsilon)\\
&\leq
\frac25(p_{21}+p_{22}-p_{51}+p_{55})
+\frac{11}{10}(1+\varepsilon).
\end{align*}
Consequently,
$$
p_{21}+p_{22}-p_{51}+p_{55}
\geq\frac{9-11\varepsilon}{4}
\geq2(1-\varepsilon),
$$
where the last inequality follows from $\varepsilon\leq1/3$.
Hence at least one of $p_{21}+p_{22}$ and $-p_{51}+p_{55}$
is at least $1-\varepsilon$, which proves \eqref{pairalternative}.\\
If $|p_{21}|+|p_{22}|\geq1-\varepsilon$, take
$$
A_1=\{1,2\},\quad k_1=2,
\qquad
A_2=\{3,4,5\},\quad k_2=4,
$$
and set
$$
x:=-u+3v
=
\Big(-1,1,\frac{11}{4},\frac{13}{4},\frac{13}{5}\Big).
$$
If instead $|p_{51}|+|p_{55}|\geq1-\varepsilon$, we take
$$
A_1=\{1,5\},\quad k_1=5,
\qquad
A_2=\{2,3,4\},\quad k_2=3,
$$
and set
$$
x:=u+3v
=
\Big(1,\frac{13}{5},\frac{13}{4},\frac{11}{4},1\Big).
$$
In either case,
$$
\sum_{j\in A_1}|p_{k_1j}|\geq1-\varepsilon.
$$
Moreover, $A_1$ and $A_2$ form a partition of $[1:5]$, and
$$
x\in V,\qquad
x_{k_2}=\|x\|_\infty=\frac{13}{4},
\qquad
|x_j|=1\quad\text{for }j\in A_1.
$$
Since $\widetilde Px=x$, we have
\begin{align*}
\frac{13}{4}
=
\Big|\sum_{j=1}^5p_{k_2j}x_j\Big|
&\leq
\sum_{j\in A_1}|p_{k_2j}|
+
\frac{13}{4}\sum_{j\in A_2}|p_{k_2j}|
=
\sum_{j=1}^5|p_{k_2j}|
+
\frac94\sum_{j\in A_2}|p_{k_2j}|\\
&\leq
1+\varepsilon
+
\frac94\sum_{j\in A_2}|p_{k_2j}|.
\end{align*}
Therefore
$\sum_{j\in A_2}|p_{k_2j}|
\geq
1-\frac49\varepsilon
\geq
1-\varepsilon.$ It remains to choose the remaining sets. Let
$A_3=\{6\},$ $k_3=6,$
and, for $j\in[1:n-3]$, set
$A_{3+j}=\{2j+5,2j+6\},$ $
k_{3+j}=2j+5.$
Since $e_6\in W_n$ and $e_{2j+5}+e_{2j+6}\in W_n,$
and $P$ is a projection onto $W_n$, we have
$$
Pe_6=e_6\qquad \textrm{and} \qquad P(e_{2j+5}+e_{2j+6})
=
e_{2j+5}+e_{2j+6}.
$$
In particular,
$$
p_{66}=1\qquad \textrm{and} \qquad
p_{2j+5,\,2j+5}+p_{2j+5,\,2j+6}=1.
$$
Hence
$\sum_{l\in A_3}|p_{k_3l}|=1$
and, for every $j\in[1:n-3]$,
$$
\sum_{l\in A_{3+j}}|p_{k_{3+j}l}|
=
|p_{2j+5,\,2j+5}|+|p_{2j+5,\,2j+6}|
\geq1.
$$
Thus all the sets $A_1,\ldots,A_n$ satisfy the required estimate,
which completes the proof.\\
~\\
The preceding proposition is not vacuous, since these spaces admit
projections of norm strictly smaller than $4/3$.
\begin{prop}\label{smallprojectionWn}
For every $n\geq3$ there exists a projection
$P_n:\ell_\infty^{2n}\to W_n$ such that
$\|P_n\|=\tfrac{13}{10}<\tfrac43.$
\end{prop}

title: Proof
body_md:
Define
$
f:=(
\tfrac23,\tfrac16,\tfrac2{15},-\tfrac2{15},-\tfrac16
),$
and $g:=(0,\frac16,\frac25,\frac25,\frac16).$
One can easily check, that
$f(u)=1,$  $f(v)=0,$ 
$g(u)=0,$ and $g(v)=1.$
Hence the operator
$Q(\cdot)=f(\cdot)u+g(\cdot)v$
is a projection from $\ell_\infty^5$ onto $V.$  The $i$-th row of $Q$
is $u_i f+v_i g$, and the sums of the absolute values of the entries
in its five rows are, respectively,
$\tfrac{190}{150}$, $\tfrac{192}{150}$, $\tfrac{195}{150}$,
$\tfrac{195}{150}$, and $\tfrac{192}{150}$. Hence
$\|Q\|=\tfrac{195}{150}=\tfrac{13}{10}.$ For $y\in\ell_\infty^5$ and
$s,a_1,b_1,\ldots,a_{n-3},b_{n-3}\in\mathbb R$, define
\begin{align*}
P_n(y,s,a_1,b_1,\ldots,a_{n-3},b_{n-3})
&:=
\Big(
Qy,s,
\tfrac{a_1+b_1}{2},\tfrac{a_1+b_1}{2},
\ldots,
\tfrac{a_{n-3}+b_{n-3}}{2},
\tfrac{a_{n-3}+b_{n-3}}{2}
\Big).
\end{align*}
Since $Q$ is a projection onto $V$, it follows directly that $P_n$
is a projection onto $W_n$. Moreover, since
$|(a_j+b_j)/2|\leq\max\{|a_j|,|b_j|\}$ and the restriction of $P_n$
to the first five coordinates is $Q$, we have
$$
\|P_n\|=\max\{\|Q\|,1\}=\frac{13}{10}<\frac43.
$$

~\\
The spaces $W_n$ show that the geometric property used above
and the column-combining condition are genuinely different.
The former fails for these spaces, whereas \eqref{colcomb} holds
for every projection onto $W_n$ of norm at most $4/3$.

So far, we have not found a counterexample to \eqref{colcomb}
among projections of norm less than $4/3$, in any codimension.
It is therefore natural to ask whether this condition holds
for every such projection onto a subspace of $\ell_\infty^N$.
By the argument of Theorem~\ref{Bazur}, this would yield the
corresponding Banach--Mazur estimate without any restriction
on the codimension. Proposition~\ref{counterhigher} shows,
however, that a general proof would require more than a direct
extension of the geometric argument used here.
